newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Budget - Review of forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Australian Budget - Review of forecasts.

text.p: Treasurer Peter Costello will deliver the Australian government's budget for 1997/98 on Tuesday at 7.30 p.m. (0930 GMT).

Below are the results of budget surveys conducted over the last two weeks -- the survey on the underlying budget deficit was conducted on Friday May 2 and the survey on the economic parameters was conducted on Friday May 9.
On the underlying deficit, economists were asked their expectations for the 1997/98 starting point deficit and what they expected Costello to announce as the target deficit.

Treasury estimated in January a no-policy change starting point of A$3.9 billion for the year to June 1998, compared with a forecast A$8.5 billion for 1996/97. Economists' median forecast was for only a slightly better starting point.

The government has signalled it is not going to repeat the heavy fiscal cuts delivered last year, and most economists expect that policy changes will reduce the deficit by about A$1.5 to A$2.0 billion.
That would still leave a small underlying deficit, although some felt that Costello would deliver a balanced budget, as was his original projection when the government won power in March 1996.
The government's current fiscal target is to eliminate the underlying budget deficit by 1998/99. On current policy settings the deficit is projected at A$2.2 billion for that year.

Economists were also asked for their forecasts of some of the budget's economic parameters. Forecasts were sought for GDP(A) growth and employment growth in year-average terms, and underlying inflation for the four quarters to June 1998.
Both GDP and employment growth are expected to be stronger than the government's latest forecasts which were contained in the mid year review released in January.
Then GDP(A) was seen at 3.5 percent and employment growth was expected to be 2.0 percent in 1997/98, although those forecasts are expected to be revised up in the Budget.

But while the economy is expected to be stronger, and the labour market to show some improvement, underlying inflation should remain comfortably within the Reserve Bank's two to three percent target range.
